vignette: The rain makes the asphalt shine like glass. He grips the handlebars, tires humming against the wet road. At thirty-three, he has memorized this commute, but tonight the streetlights blur. The truck runs the red light. There is no time to brake. The world tilts, metal groans, and the impact throws him forward. The airbag deployment hits his chest like a fist. Then, static. He wakes in the ICU with a fractured tibia and right wrist, but the fracture he cannot see runs deeper. In the weeks that follow, his bones knit while his mind refuses to settle. The rhythmic beeping of the cardiac monitor becomes a trigger that makes his throat close and his pulse spike. He stops riding. He stops taking the backroads home. He tells his wife, Lena, that he is taking the bus until he feels steady. Sleep fractures into fragments. He dreams of the skid, the sound of tearing leather, the way the sky spun above him. He wakes gasping, hands already reaching for his phone to check on her, even though she sleeps quietly beside him. He was raised in a South Eastern Asian household that prized quiet endurance, yet now he cannot ignore the tremor in his hands. At the clinic, he works as a physical therapist. He guides patients through range-of-motion exercises, explains nerve glides, and adjusts gait belts. But his own body feels like a foreign document he no longer trusts. When a patient's chair rolls backward with a squeak, his shoulders snap up. When a colleague drops a metal tray in the hallway, his stomach drops. He finds himself standing near exits during team meetings, scanning the room. He reorganizes his treatment rooms, moving chairs away from windows, keeping his hands busy with towels and resistance bands to ground himself during the day. He stays late, folding charts because stillness invites the replay: the impact, the silence, the narrow margin between consciousness and the void. Lena notices the distance. She touches his shoulder to ask about dinner, and he tenses before remembering who she is. They speak about it sometimes, but the words always seem to hit a wall of fog. He loves her fiercely, yet he sleeps in the guest room two nights a week, saying it is for his back. He knows it is because the sound of her breathing makes him acutely aware of how fragile time can be. He watches her laugh with friends and feels a quiet ache of separation, as though he is living in a room with the windows sealed shut. He treats patients. He pays bills. He smiles when expected. But beneath the routine, his nervous system runs a perpetual background scan: Is anything moving too fast? Is the road clear? Is this moment safe? Today, he sits at his desk after the last appointment. The clinic is quiet. Rain begins to tap against the high windows. He rests his hands on the keyboard, watching the droplets slide down the glass. His breath is steady now. He knows the fear will return when the next storm rolls in, when a car backfires near the clinic, when a patient's gait reminds him of a lost balance. He carries it all, not as a failure, but as a weight he has learned to shift, step by step, through the quiet architecture of his days.
